messages.author: 872f23514ec95bf7
messages.subject: Constant scale values not inherited
parts:
Dear list members,

Please see the following examples:

qplot(Petal.Length, Petal.Width, data=iris, colour=Species, size=I(4)) + geom_jitter()
qplot(Petal.Length, Petal.Width, data=iris, colour=Species, pch=I(2)) + geom_jitter()

It looks like only the non-jittered points ‘inherit’ the size and shape
values. It looks like a bug to me, but perhaps the ‘contant’ values are
only *supposed* to apply to points? For example, using geom_path(),

qplot(Petal.Length, Petal.Width, data=iris, colour=Species, size=I(4)) + geom_path()

only the points change size, not the lines. Note that using
geom="jitter" or geom="path" *inside* qplot, things work as expected.

So, is this non-inheritance of constant/literal values a feature or a
bug?

--
Karl Ove Hufthammer

I prefer the ggplot notation over the qplot notation. A bit more verbose, but with clear code.

ggplot(iris, aes(x = Petal.Length, y = Petal.Width, colour = Species)) + geom_jitter(size = 4)
ggplot(iris, aes(x = Petal.Length, y = Petal.Width, colour = Species)) + geom_jitter(shape = 2)
ggplot(iris, aes(x = Petal.Length, y = Petal.Width, colour = Species)) + geom_path(size = 2)

messages.author: 0c39e60ddb38622b
messages.subject: Re: Constant scale values not inherited
parts:
Hi:

Thierry showed you how to do it the right way, but it may be helpful
to examine what happens with your code. It's sufficient to look at the
first example. Without geom_jitter(), the qplot() call produces a
scatterplot, which is equivalent to

qplot(Petal.Length, Petal.Width, data = iris, geom = 'point', colour =
Species, size = I(4))

geom_jitter() is a combination of geom_point() with the position
adjustment function position_jitter(). Essentially, your code is
requesting that the first layer in the graphic be geom_point() and the
second layer geom_jitter(), which is at least partially redundant. In
part, this is why you get confusing results.

In contrast, Thierry's code using ggplot() first sets up the common
aesthetics and then calls geom_jitter() to produce a single layer of
jittered points using a set value of the aesthetic to be jittered
(size, shape or path). The ggplot() call defines the ggplot object
(data and common [mapped] aesthetics to be used), but contains no
layers in and of itself; geom_jitter() provides the necessary layer.

Going back to qplot(), had you used

qplot(Petal.Length, Petal.Width, data = iris, geom = 'jitter', colour
= Species, size = I(4))
qplot(Petal.Length, Petal.Width, data=iris, geom = 'jitter',
colour=Species, shape = I(2))

you would have been OK. This is suggested by Thierry's ggplot() code.

HTH,
Dennis

  qplot(Petal.Length, Petal.Width, data=iris, colour=Species, size=I(4)) + geom_path()

only the points change size, not the lines. Note that using

I am dredging this up from a few months ago since I have come across this too and it seems a true problem or at least unexpected and not just a matter of using ggplot vs. qplot as suggested by some of the responders.  In the jitter code example that was used in this thread the layer does not inherit size=4 so

ggplot(iris, aes(Petal.Length, Petal.Width), size = 4) + geom_jitter()

is not identical to:

ggplot(iris, aes(Petal.Length, Petal.Width)) + geom_jitter(size = 4)

I would have expected both to give the same answer based on the idea that the layers inherit defaults from the ggplot() args.

The argument in favor of having all ggplot() arguments be inherited by the layers is simplicity.  

One could then have a more compact description of how it works.  Namely ggplot() could inherit globals and then layers could inherit from ggplot like this (where we have termed settings that are set via update_geom_defaults as globals):

   globals <- ggplot() <- layers. 

Right now layers inherit some things from globals set via update_geom_defaults() and some things from ggplot() so it looks like this (at least conceptually - this may not be how it works internally):

   globals <- layers
   ggplot() <- layers

which is harder to understand since one would need to remember which is inherited from which.

Ideally one could just say that layers inherit from ggplot() which inherits from the global defaults.
